strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across four diverse benchmarks (HotpotQA, IFBench, HoVer, PUPA) and two models (Qwen3-8B, GPT-4.1 mini), with consistent gains over both GRPO and MIPROv2.

Well-motivated method combining reflective natural-language feedback, genetic/evolutionary prompt mutation, and Pareto-frontier-based candidate selection to avoid local optima; the ablation (SelectBestCandidate vs Pareto sampling) convincingly demonstrates the value of this design choice.
Strong sample-efficiency story, with rollout budgets matched to MIPROv2 for fairness and detailed rollout accounting (train vs validation) that is transparent about where budget is spent.
Rich supplementary material: full search trees, complete prompt evolution trajectories, and actual optimized prompts for every benchmark/model, which aids reproducibility and interpretability.

Additional exploratory results on using GEPA as an inference-time search strategy for kernel/CUDA code generation (NPUEval, KernelBench) broaden the demonstrated applicability beyond prompt optimization for QA-style tasks.
Honest discussion of limitations (e.g., LoRA-only GRPO baseline, lack of few-shot exemplar optimization, inconsistent benefit of the Merge strategy) and clear directions for future work.
weaknesses: The comparison to GRPO may be somewhat unfair/apples-to-oranges: GRPO is only run with LoRA and limited hyperparameter search (500 steps, fixed budget), while prompt optimization and RL address different resource trade-offs (inference-time prompt length vs weight updates); the strong title claim ('can outperform RL') may overstate generality given this specific, constrained RL setup.

Method novelty is somewhat incremental — it combines existing ideas (LLM-based reflective prompt rewriting, evolutionary/genetic search, Pareto-optimal MAP-Elites-style illumination, textual environment feedback) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; several of these components have precedents (EvoPrompt, MAP-Elites, DSPy/MIPROv2, TextGrad).

GEPA+Merge results are inconsistent (helps for GPT-4.1 mini but sometimes hurts for Qwen3-8B), and the authors admit hyperparameters for when/how often to invoke merge were not tuned per model, weakening confidence in this component's generalizability.

Some qualitative examples in the appendix show GEPA leaving certain modules essentially unchanged from the seed prompt (e.g., summarize1/summarize2 for HotpotQA/HoVer with GPT-4.1 mini), suggesting uneven optimization across modules that isn't fully analyzed.

Inference-time search results (NPUEval, KernelBench) are explicitly called 'preliminary' with limited task counts and no strong baselines beyond simple RAG/MIPROv2 variants, so their generalizability is unclear.

The generalization-gap analysis and prompt-length efficiency claims, while interesting, are somewhat secondary observations not rigorously ablated (e.g., no controlled study isolating why shorter GEPA prompts generalize better beyond correlation).

strengths: The paper tackles a practically relevant problem (sample-efficient adaptation of compound LLM systems) and proposes a reasonably coherent system (GEPA) combining reflective natural-language mutation with a Pareto-frontier-based candidate-selection strategy, which is a sensible evolutionary-search design.

The empirical protocol is fairly detailed: train/val/test splits are described, rollout budgets are matched between GEPA and MIPROv2, and hyperparameters for GRPO/LoRA are specified, aiding partial reproducibility.

The ablation comparing Pareto-based sampling against a naive SelectBestCandidate strategy, together with the visualized search trees (Figs. 6, 17-24), gives some genuine insight into why the proposed illumination strategy helps avoid local optima.
The appendix provides full optimized prompts and search trajectories, which is useful for understanding qualitatively what the reflective mutation step is producing.

The paper reports results across two models (open-source Qwen3-8B and proprietary GPT-4.1-mini) and four tasks, plus exploratory extensions to code-optimization domains, which is a reasonably broad evaluation surface for a prompt-optimization paper.
weaknesses: The paper's central, title-level claim ('reflective prompt evolution can outperform reinforcement learning') rests on a single RL baseline (GRPO with LoRA rank 16, fixed at 24,000 rollouts, limited manual hyperparameter search) trained on only 150 examples per task. The authors themselves note in the limitations that full-parameter GRPO is not tested and that prior GRPO work commonly uses 100k-512k rollouts, which directly undercuts the rollout-efficiency comparison and makes the headline claim appear calibrated to a setting designed to favor GEPA rather than a fair, representative RL comparison.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported for any of the main results (Table 1, Table 2), despite GEPA, MIPROv2, and GRPO all being stochastic optimization procedures over relatively small test sets (221-300 examples). Reported gaps (e.g., GEPA+Merge dropping IFBench Qwen3 score from 38.6 to 28.2) suggest high run-to-run variance that is never quantified, making it hard to trust the magnitude of reported improvements.

The 'fair rollout budget' comparison between GEPA and MIPROv2/GRPO ignores that a large majority of GEPA's counted rollouts are spent on Pareto-set validation rather than learning signal (acknowledged by the authors), and that MIPROv2's optimized prompts are much longer (up to 9.2x) and thus incur higher per-call inference cost; neither token-level nor wall-clock compute cost is controlled for, so the 'sample efficiency' narrative is not a clean apples-to-apples comparison.

The core algorithmic ingredients (LLM-based reflective textual feedback for prompt mutation, evolutionary/genetic search, Pareto/MAP-Elites-style illumination for diversity) are individually well established in prior work (EvoPrompt, PromptBreeder, APE, MIPROv2, Dynamic Cheatsheet, AlphaEvolve); the contribution is primarily an engineering combination for compound multi-module systems rather than a fundamentally new technique, which somewhat limits novelty relative to the strength of the claims made.

GEPA+Merge is shown to sometimes substantially hurt performance (e.g., IFBench with Qwen3 drops ~10 points versus GEPA alone), and the authors admit the crossover hyperparameters were not tuned per-model; this inconsistency, combined with the lack of a principled stopping/merge-invocation criterion, suggests the proposed 'system-aware merge' is not yet a reliable component despite being prominently advertised in the abstract and results tables.

The additional inference-time search experiments (NPUEval, KernelBench) are explicitly labeled 'preliminary,' use only Best-of-N/single-seed comparisons without proper baselines matched for cost, and are evaluated on a small/early benchmark version and a 35-task 'representative subset,' yet they are used to generate strong qualitative claims (e.g., '70% vector utilization') that are not adequately substantiated by rigorous evaluation.

The benchmark suite (HotpotQA, HoVer, IFBench, PUPA) is composed entirely of retrieval/instruction-following/privacy-delegation tasks with relatively small training sets (111-150 examples); there is no evaluation on the math/code/agentic reasoning benchmarks where GRPO and RLVR methods are most commonly and successfully applied in the literature the paper itself cites, limiting the generality of the 'outperforms RL' claim.

Comparisons are limited to only two baselines (MIPROv2 and GRPO); other relevant compound-system optimizers discussed in related work (TextGrad, Optimas, PromptBreeder, EvoPrompt, DSPy's COPRO) are never empirically compared against, despite being readily available baselines for prompt-based optimization.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and reasonably novel optimizer (GEPA) that combines LLM-based reflective textual feedback with genetic/Pareto-based multi-objective candidate selection for optimizing compound AI systems, clearly differentiated from prior work (EvoPrompt, MIPROv2, AlphaEvolve, TextGrad, DSPy).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 4 diverse tasks (HotpotQA, IFBench, HoVer, PUPA) and two model families (Qwen3-8B, GPT-4.1-mini), with consistent and substantial gains over both a leading prompt optimizer (MIPROv2) and an RL baseline (GRPO).
Strong and practically important result: large sample-efficiency gains (up to 35x fewer rollouts) relative to GRPO, which is valuable for rollout-constrained real-world settings.

Thoughtful ablation isolating the contribution of Pareto-based candidate selection vs. greedy best-candidate selection, with clear qualitative (search tree) and quantitative evidence that Pareto sampling avoids local optima.

Extensive supplementary materials (full search trees, optimized prompts, generalization-gap analysis, prompt-length/cost analysis) that aid interpretability and reproducibility of the qualitative claims.

Promising additional demonstration of generality by applying GEPA to inference-time code optimization (NPUEval, KernelBench), suggesting the method's applicability beyond the primary prompt-optimization setting.
Honest discussion of limitations (e.g., validation-set rollout overhead, inconsistent benefits of the Merge strategy across models, unresolved prompt- vs weight-based learning boundary).
weaknesses: The GRPO baseline uses LoRA with limited/manual hyperparameter search and a comparatively small rollout budget (24k) relative to the hundreds of thousands of rollouts the paper itself cites as typical for GRPO elsewhere; this may understate RL's potential ceiling and makes the 'RL is less sample efficient' claim somewhat asymmetric.

Benchmarks use fairly small training sets (111-150 examples) and moderate-complexity tasks; it's unclear how GEPA's reflective mutation and Pareto bookkeeping scale to much larger training sets, more modules, or noisier reward signals.
No variance/seed analysis or statistical significance testing is reported for the main results, which is important given the stochastic nature of both LLM-based mutation and evolutionary search.

GEPA+Merge yields inconsistent and sometimes negative results (e.g., degrades performance on Qwen3-8B), and the same fixed hyperparameters were used across models without tuning, weakening the rigor of conclusions about the crossover strategy.

Matching MIPROv2 and GEPA rollout budgets is only approximate (up to ~10% discrepancy), and MIPROv2's heavy auto-setting/few-shot bootstrapping may not be optimally configured for this low-data, budget-matched regime, raising some concern about comparison fairness.

The method depends on carefully engineered per-task feedback functions (module-level diagnostic text), which requires nontrivial manual effort per domain and is in tension with claims of broad, automatic applicability.

The inference-time code-optimization results (NPUEval, KernelBench) are explicitly preliminary, based on a small number of tasks and limited baselines, and should be read as suggestive rather than conclusive evidence of generality.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 6 diverse benchmarks (multi-hop QA, math, instruction following, privacy-aware delegation, claim verification) and 2 models (open-source Qwen3-8B and proprietary GPT-4.1-Mini), providing strong evidence for the method's generality.

Strong and relevant baseline comparisons, including GRPO (with matched/fixed rollout budgets and both LoRA and full-parameter finetuning variants), MIPROv2, TextGrad, and Trace/OptoPrime, giving a comprehensive picture of where GEPA sits relative to both RL and prior prompt-optimization methods.

Well-designed ablation studies isolating the contribution of the Pareto-based candidate selection strategy versus greedy (SelectBestCandidate) and beam-search baselines, with clear visualizations of search trees showing how Pareto sampling avoids local optima.
Rollout-budget-matched comparisons with MIPROv2 make the efficiency claims more credible than an unconstrained comparison would.

Additional exploratory applications (NPU/CUDA kernel inference-time search, adversarial prompt search) demonstrate the versatility of the framework and add practical value beyond the core prompt-optimization claim.

Thorough appendix with full optimized prompts, algorithmic details (Merge/crossover procedure), cost analysis, generalization-gap analysis, and rollout-vs-performance curves supports reproducibility and transparency.

Interesting and non-obvious finding that instruction-only reflective optimization can outperform joint instruction+few-shot optimization, contrasting with prior work, and the explanation offered (via generalization-gap comparison) is thoughtful.
Cross-model transfer experiment (prompts optimized on Qwen3-8B transferring to GPT-4.1-Mini) is a nice additional demonstration of robustness.
weaknesses: The central 'outperforms RL' claim rests on a GRPo configuration (24k rollouts, LoRA, specific hyperparameters) that, despite the full-finetuning appendix check, may still not represent a fully tuned/compute-matched RL baseline; RL is typically deployed with far larger budgets and more extensive hyperparameter search in practice, so the comparison, while informative, should be interpreted as favorable-case rather than a definitive verdict.

No variance/statistical significance reporting across multiple seeds or runs is provided for the main results tables; given LLM-based reflection and stochastic search, run-to-run variability could be non-trivial and is not quantified.

Core algorithmic ideas (genetic/evolutionary prompt search, reflection on trajectories, Pareto/quality-diversity based selection) each have clear precedents in prior literature (EvoPrompt, Promptbreeder, MAP-Elites/quality-diversity, Reflexion, TextGrad); the novelty is primarily in the specific combination and engineering rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The Merge/crossover strategy shows inconsistent benefits across models (helps GPT-4.1-Mini, often hurts Qwen3-8B) and the authors acknowledge hyperparameters were not tuned per model, leaving this component under-validated.

The inference-time search (NPUEval/KernelBench) and adversarial prompt search sections are explicitly labeled preliminary, use single-model exploratory setups without strong baselines/ablations, and are somewhat tangential to the paper's main thesis, diluting focus.

The adversarial prompt search result shows the model outputting a literal placeholder ('### <final answer>'), suggesting the large performance drop may partly reflect a formatting/parsing artifact rather than purely semantic distraction, which weakens the interpretability of that case study.

Reflection/mutation cost (number of reflection LM calls, meta-prompt overhead) is reported but its monetary/latency cost relative to GRPO training cost is not deeply analyzed, making the full efficiency picture only partially complete.

strengths: Introduces a practically useful system (GEPA) that combines reflective natural-language feedback with genetic/Pareto-based candidate selection for optimizing prompts in compound AI systems, and clearly articulates the design rationale (Pareto frontier vs. greedy/beam search) with supporting ablations (Table 3, Figure 6).

Broad empirical coverage: 6 diverse tasks (multi-hop QA, math, instruction following, privacy-aware delegation, fact verification) across two models (open-source Qwen3-8B and closed-source GPT-4.1-mini), with consistent improvements over MIPROv2 and reasonable transparency about rollout budgets and costs.
Thoughtful ablations isolating the contribution of Pareto-based candidate selection versus naive best-candidate or beam-search strategies, showing a clear and consistent benefit.

Interesting additional demonstrations of the method's generality as an inference-time search strategy for kernel code optimization (NPUEval, KernelBench) and for adversarial prompt discovery, broadening the paper's potential impact beyond prompt optimization alone.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendix with full prompts, algorithm boxes, hyperparameters, and cost breakdowns.
weaknesses: The headline claim that reflective prompt evolution 'can outperform reinforcement learning' rests on a GRPO baseline trained with a fixed 24k-rollout budget and hyperparameters only manually explored over a few values; the intro itself notes that typical RLVR works use up to hundreds of thousands of rollouts, so the RL baseline may be substantially under-tuned/under-trained relative to standard practice, making the 'outperforms RL' framing somewhat overstated.

Comparing prompt-space optimization (GEPA) to weight-space optimization (GRPO) on 'rollout count' alone conflates fundamentally different cost structures (e.g., GRPO rollouts include gradient updates and are not directly comparable to inference-only GEPA rollouts in wall-clock or compute terms); the paper acknowledges validation overhead dominates GEPA's own rollout budget, which further muddies the efficiency comparison.

Inspection of the optimized prompts in the appendix (e.g., HotpotQA final-answer module) reveals what appear to be memorized or near-verbatim factual answers to specific validation/training questions (e.g., hardcoded nicknames, company types) embedded directly into the 'instructions' — this raises concern that some reported gains reflect a form of train-time memorization/overfitting into the prompt rather than purely generalizable reasoning strategies, which is in tension with the paper's generalization claims (Observation 2, Figure 16).

GEPA+Merge shows inconsistent and sometimes harmful effects (hurting performance on 3/4 Qwen3-8B tasks), and the paper admits hyperparameters were not tuned per model/task, leaving the method's practical reliability under-explored.

Several evaluation sets are quite small (e.g., 30-question AIME-2025 test set, ~220-300 instance splits for other tasks), and most reported numbers appear to be single runs without variance/confidence intervals, limiting confidence in the statistical significance of reported differences, especially for closely-spaced baselines.

The inference-time search and adversarial prompt sections (Sections 5.1–5.2) are explicitly described as 'preliminary' and are evaluated with limited scope (single adversarial example walkthrough, small kernel benchmarks), so they read more as promising anecdotes than rigorous additional contributions.

strengths: Strong empirical results showing GEPA outperforms GRPO with substantially fewer rollouts across six benchmarks and two model families
Thorough ablation of the Pareto-based candidate selection strategy versus greedy/beam-search alternatives, clearly isolating the source of gains
Comparison against multiple strong, relevant baselines (MIPROv2, TextGrad, Trace/OptoPrime, GRPO with LoRA and full fine-tuning)
Extensive reproducibility materials including full prompts, hyperparameters, costs, and optimization trees in the appendix
Practical findings on prompt compactness/cost efficiency and cross-model transfer of optimized prompts
Interesting additional applications (inference-time search for kernel generation, adversarial prompt discovery) demonstrating generality of the approach
weaknesses: GRPO baseline tuning effort and rollout budget matching methodology could be more rigorously justified to ensure a fully fair comparison
Only two models evaluated (Qwen3-8B, GPT-4.1 Mini), leaving open questions about scaling behavior with larger/smaller or weaker instruction-following models
Kernel generation and adversarial search sections are explicitly preliminary with limited quantitative rigor and single-model evaluation
Reflection LM overhead (additional LLM calls for reflection) is not deeply analyzed in terms of wall-clock cost versus RL training cost
GEPA+Merge shows inconsistent benefits across models (helps GPT-4.1 Mini, often hurts Qwen3-8B), indicating the merge component is less mature than the core algorithm
Minor text/encoding artifacts in the appendix suggest the manuscript could benefit from additional polishing
